title: Set Operations
short: Union, intersection, difference and complement, pictured with Venn diagrams, with De Morgan's laws for sets.
trouble: Students take the complement of A ∩ B to be Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ instead of Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ.

blocks.html: In probability you combined events with "or," "and" and "not." Events are sets of outcomes, so those were set operations all along. Here they get their general names and notation, building on sets and subsets.

For sets inside a universe $U$: the union $A \cup B$ is everything in $A$ or $B$ (or both); the intersection $A \cap B$ is everything in both; the difference $A \setminus B$ is what is in $A$ but not $B$; the complement $A^{c} = U \setminus A$ is everything in $U$ not in $A$. De Morgan's laws hold for sets: $(A \cup B)^{c} = A^{c} \cap B^{c}$ and $(A \cap B)^{c} = A^{c} \cup B^{c}$.

Each operation is a logical connective applied to membership. $x \in A \cup B$ means $x \in A \vee x \in B$; $x \in A \cap B$ means $x \in A \wedge x \in B$; $x \in A^{c}$ means $\neg(x \in A)$. So every logical equivalence becomes a set identity. De Morgan's laws for sets are the same laws you proved with truth tables, with "or" and "and" replaced by $\cup$ and $\cap$. (Probability books often write $A'$ for the complement; it means the same as $A^{c}$.)

blocks.name: venn
blocks.cap: Tap regions, or pick an event. Compare $(A \cap B)'$ with $A' \cap B'$: they are different regions. (This visual writes the complement as $A'$.)

blocks.title: Computing with a universe
blocks.q: Let $U = \{1, 2, \ldots, 10\}$, $A = \{2, 4, 6, 8, 10\}$ (the even numbers) and $B = \{3, 6, 9\}$ (the multiples of $3$). Find $A \cup B$, $A \cap B$, $A \setminus B$, $A^{c}$ and $(A \cup B)^{c}$.

blocks.title: Sizes with De Morgan
blocks.q: In a universe of $40$ people, $|A| = 18$, $|B| = 15$ and $|A \cap B| = 6$. How many people are in $A^{c} \cup B^{c}$?
steps: So the count is everyone except the $6$ people in both: $40 - 6 = 34$.

blocks.html: Complementing each piece without switching the operation. $(A \cap B)^{c}$ is not $A^{c} \cap B^{c}$. To be outside "both $A$ and $B$," you only need to miss one of them, so $(A \cap B)^{c} = A^{c} \cup B^{c}$. Check with one element: in the example above, $3$ is in $(A \cap B)^{c}$ (it is not in both), but $3$ is not in $A^{c} \cap B^{c}$ (it is in $B$).
